turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: I want to start with a field on a form. Cultural needs. And the answer, again and again, is none identified.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: Honestly, that question feels awkward to ask. People usually mention what matters to them.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Usually they don't, at least not to someone from an agency. And Minnesota law treats it as part of the process. For people using waiver services, informed decision making includes identification of the person's cultural needs and access to culturally responsive services and providers.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: So how do you ask without it being awkward or stereotyping?

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Open questions about what matters. What's important to you in how people help you at home? Anything about your faith, food or routines helpers should know? Who do you want with you when decisions are made? Which language are you most comfortable in?

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: And not, people from that community usually prefer this.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Exactly. Background can suggest a question. It never answers it.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: Say the person wants helpers who speak their language, and there aren't any in the county.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Widen the search. Ask navigators and community organizations what they know. Ask providers specific questions about what they could adapt. Bring the options back and let the person choose. And record honestly what you looked for and didn't find.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Because a hidden gap never gets fixed. One record is a person's story. A pattern of the same gap is something the program can act on.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Be specific, in the person's words. Prefers family tells a new helper almost nothing. Wants their sister present for decisions, prefers a female helper for bathing, tells them what to do. And ask again when life changes.
